lead: LPI's first professional Linux cert, earned over two exams. It proves you can run a Linux system from the command line: install software, manage disks, users and services, read logs, set up networking and lock the box down. It's vendor-neutral, so it works on Ubuntu, Red Hat and the Linux servers behind most clouds.
objSub: LPIC-1 is two exams. Switch between 101 and 102 above; each has its own topics and its own progress. Tick objectives as you study; your progress stays on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan covers both exams, about 70 hours each: topics split by exam weight, then a practice stretch before each test.

e101.label: Exam 101
e101.note: System architecture, installing Linux and managing packages, GNU and Unix commands, and devices, file systems and the directory layout. Commands are almost half of this exam. You can take 101 and 102 in either order.
e101.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 5.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 60 questions it gets. LPI removed 104.4, so the numbers skip it.

domains.name: System Architecture
obj: Determine and configure hardware settings
Weight 2. Enable devices, read hardware info from /sys, /proc and /dev, and use lsmod, modprobe, lspci and lsusb.
Boot the system
Weight 3. Firmware to boot loader to kernel to init; SysVinit vs systemd; read boot messages with dmesg and journalctl.
Change runlevels / boot targets and shutdown or reboot
Weight 3. Set the default target, switch targets (including rescue), shutdown, reboot and wall.

domains.name: Linux Installation and Package Management
obj: Design hard disk layout
Weight 2. Partitions for /, /var, /home and /boot, the EFI system partition, swap and basic LVM.
Install a boot manager
Weight 2. GRUB 2 basics: grub-install, grub-mkconfig, and editing boot options.
Manage shared libraries
Weight 1. ldd, ldconfig, /etc/ld.so.conf and LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
Use Debian package management
Weight 3. dpkg, apt-get and apt-cache: install, remove, find which package owns a file, list a package's files.
Use RPM and YUM package management
Weight 3. rpm, yum, dnf and zypper: install, query, verify signatures and map files to packages.
Linux as a virtualization guest
Weight 1. VMs vs containers, cloud instances, what to change on a cloned VM (SSH host keys, machine ID), cloud-init.

domains.name: GNU and Unix Commands
obj: Work on the command line
Weight 4. Variables, export, env, set, history, type and which, and running programs inside and outside PATH.
Process text streams using filters
Weight 2. cat, cut, sort, uniq, tr, head, tail, wc, sed, nl, split, zcat, and checksums with sha256sum.
Perform basic file management
Weight 4. cp, mv, rm, mkdir, find by type, size and time, tar, cpio, dd, gzip, bzip2 and xz.
Use streams, pipes and redirects
Weight 4. Redirect stdin, stdout and stderr; pipes; tee and xargs.
Create, monitor and kill processes
Weight 4. Jobs with &, bg, fg and nohup; ps, top, pgrep; signals with kill, pkill and killall; screen and tmux.
Modify process execution priorities
Weight 2. nice and renice; reading priority in ps and top.
Search text files using regular expressions
Weight 3. Basic vs extended regex; grep, grep -E and sed substitutions.
Basic file editing
Weight 3. vi modes, moving, editing, searching and saving (:w, :q!, ZZ); setting EDITOR.

domains.name: Devices, Linux Filesystems, Filesystem Hierarchy Standard
obj: Create partitions and filesystems
Weight 2. MBR and GPT with fdisk, gdisk and parted; mkfs for ext4, XFS, VFAT and exFAT; mkswap.
Maintain the integrity of filesystems
Weight 2. df and du for space and inodes; fsck, e2fsck, tune2fs and xfs_repair.
Control mounting and unmounting of filesystems
Weight 3. mount, umount, /etc/fstab, UUIDs and labels with blkid and lsblk; systemd mount units.
Manage file permissions and ownership
Weight 3. chmod, chown, chgrp and umask; SUID, SGID and the sticky bit.
Create and change hard and symbolic links
Weight 2. ln and ln -s; hard vs soft links; copy vs link.
Find system files and place files in the correct location
Weight 2. The FHS layout; find, locate and updatedb, whereis, which and type.

e102.label: Exam 102
e102.note: Shells and scripting, desktops and accessibility, admin tasks like users, cron and time zones, essential services (time, logging, mail, printing), networking and security.
e102.onote: Official LPI objectives, version 5.0. Each objective's weight is about how many of the 60 questions it gets.

domains.name: Shells and Shell Scripting
obj: Customize and use the shell environment
Weight 4. /etc/profile, ~/.bashrc and ~/.bash_profile, aliases, functions, export and source; /etc/skel.
Customize or write simple scripts
Weight 4. for, while, if and test, read, seq, command substitution, exit codes, && and ||, and the shebang.

domains.name: User Interfaces and Desktops
obj: Install and configure X11
Weight 2. X11 vs Wayland, xorg.conf, DISPLAY, xhost and xauth.
Graphical Desktops
Weight 1. KDE, GNOME and Xfce; remote desktops with VNC, RDP, Spice and XDMCP.
Accessibility
Weight 1. High contrast and large print, screen readers, magnifiers, on-screen keyboards, sticky and slow keys.

domains.name: Administrative Tasks
obj: Manage user and group accounts and related system files
Weight 5, the heaviest objective. useradd, usermod, userdel, groupadd, passwd, chage and getent; /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group.
Automate system administration tasks by scheduling jobs
Weight 4. crontab and /etc/cron.*, at, cron.allow and cron.deny, and systemd timers.
Localisation and internationalisation
Weight 3. Locales (LANG, LC_ALL), time zones with timedatectl and /etc/localtime, UTF-8 and iconv.

domains.name: Essential System Services
obj: Maintain system time
Weight 3. date, hwclock and timedatectl; NTP with chrony or ntpd.
System logging
Weight 4. rsyslog facilities and priorities, logger, logrotate, and querying the journal with journalctl.
Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) basics
Weight 3. Aliases and forwarding with ~/.forward and newaliases; mail and mailq; Postfix, Sendmail and Exim.
Manage printers and printing
Weight 2. CUPS, lpr, lpq and lprm.

domains.name: Networking Fundamentals
obj: Fundamentals of internet protocols
Weight 4. Subnetting and CIDR, private ranges, TCP vs UDP vs ICMP, common ports, IPv4 vs IPv6.
Persistent network configuration
Weight 4. NetworkManager and nmcli, hostnamectl, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/nsswitch.conf.
Basic network troubleshooting
Weight 4. ip, ss, ping, traceroute, tracepath and netcat; the older ifconfig, netstat and route.
Configure client side DNS
Weight 2. host, dig and getent; resolution order; systemd-resolved.

domains.name: Security
obj: Perform security administration tasks
Weight 3. Find SUID and SGID files, password aging, open ports (ss, lsof, nmap), ulimit, who is logged in, and sudo.
Setup host security
Weight 3. Shadow passwords, turning off unused services, /etc/nologin, TCP wrappers.
Securing data with encryption
Weight 4. OpenSSH client and keys (ssh-keygen, ssh-agent), host keys, SSH tunnels, and GnuPG to encrypt, sign and verify.

method: Use the topics above as your checklist, one exam at a time. Topic 103 (commands) is 43% of exam 101.
Work through LPI's free Learning Materials objective by objective. Add a study guide book for depth.
Run two VMs: one Debian or Ubuntu, one Rocky Linux. The exams test both package families, and you only learn the differences by using both.
Flashcards for command options, config file paths, signals, cron fields and ports.
Timed 60-question sets in 90 minutes. For every fill-in-the-blank you miss, type the command in a VM until it's right.
tips: Some questions make you type a command or path with no options to pick from. Spelling counts.
If a question doesn't name the distro, think about whether it's asking for the Debian or the RPM tool.
Redirection order (2>&1), cron fields and find tests are easy to get backwards. Slow down on them.
There's no penalty for guessing, so always answer.

quiz.q: A server boots to a graphical login. From now on it should boot to a text console with networking. Which command makes that change?
o: systemctl set-default multi-user.target
Right. set-default changes the target used at every boot.
systemctl isolate multi-user.target
isolate switches to that target right now, but the next boot goes back to the GUI.
telinit 3
The old SysVinit way to switch runlevels now. It doesn't change the default for future boots.
systemctl enable multi-user.target
enable is for units with an install section, like services. It doesn't set the default boot target.

quiz.q: On an Ubuntu server, which command tells you which installed package owns /usr/bin/ssh?
o: dpkg -S /usr/bin/ssh
Right. dpkg -S searches installed packages for the file and names the owner.
rpm -qf /usr/bin/ssh
That's the right idea on Red Hat-family systems, but Ubuntu uses dpkg.
dpkg -L /usr/bin/ssh
-L lists the files in a package you name. It expects a package name, not a file path.
apt-cache search ssh
That searches package descriptions in the repositories, not which installed package owns a file.

quiz.q: You suspect a web shell was dropped on a web server. Which command lists regular files under /var/www that were MODIFIED in the last 24 hours?
o: find /var/www -type f -mtime -1
Right. -mtime -1 means changed less than one day ago, and -type f limits it to regular files.
find /var/www -type f -mtime +1
+1 means MORE than one day ago, the opposite of what you want.
find /var/www -type f -atime -1
-atime is the last ACCESS time. Every visitor reading a page changes it, and it doesn't show changes.
locate -mtime -1 /var/www
locate searches a name database. It has no time filters.

quiz.q: Which command sends BOTH the normal output and the error messages of ./scan.sh into scan.log?
o: ./scan.sh > scan.log 2>&1
Right. Redirects run left to right: stdout goes to the file, then stderr is pointed wherever stdout now goes.
./scan.sh 2>&1 > scan.log
Order matters. stderr is copied to the terminal BEFORE stdout moves to the file, so errors still print on screen.
./scan.sh > scan.log 2> scan.log
The file is opened twice separately, so the two streams overwrite each other and the log gets garbled.
./scan.sh | tee scan.log
A pipe carries only stdout. The errors still print on screen and never reach the file.

quiz.q: You start a long packet capture over SSH and it must keep running after you log out. Which is the BEST way to start it?
o: nohup tcpdump -w cap.pcap &
Right. nohup makes it ignore the hangup signal sent at logout, and & runs it in the background. (screen or tmux also work.)
tcpdump -w cap.pcap &
It runs in the background but can still be killed by the hangup signal when your session ends.
Start it, press Ctrl+Z, then type bg
That moves it to the background, but it's still tied to your session.
nice -n 19 tcpdump -w cap.pcap
nice only lowers its priority. It doesn't protect it from your logout.

quiz.q: Which command replaces EVERY http:// with https:// in urls.txt and saves the change in the file itself?
o: sed -i 's|http://|https://|g' urls.txt
Right. -i edits the file in place and g replaces every match on each line. Using | as the delimiter avoids escaping the slashes.
sed 's|http://|https://|g' urls.txt
Without -i, sed prints the changed text to the screen and leaves the file alone.
sed -i 's|http://|https://|' urls.txt
Without g, only the first match on each line is replaced.
grep -E 's/http/https/' urls.txt
grep only finds lines. It can't substitute text.

quiz.q: What does the s in this listing mean, and why do security reviewers care about it?
o: SUID: the program runs with its owner's (root's) rights, so any flaw in it can become root access
Right. passwd needs root to update /etc/shadow. An unexpected SUID-root file is a common privilege-escalation path.
The sticky bit: only the owner can delete the file
The sticky bit shows as t in the others position, and it matters on directories like /tmp.
SGID: it runs with the group's rights
SGID shows as s in the GROUP position (----rws---). Here it's in the owner position.
It's a socket file
A socket shows s as the FIRST character (srwx...). This one starts with -, a regular file.

quiz.q: A new data disk must mount at /data at every boot, even if its device name changes from sdb1 to sdc1. What should the /etc/fstab line use to identify it?
o: UUID=… (find it with blkid or lsblk -f)
Right. The UUID is stored in the file system itself and never changes when disks are added or reordered.
/dev/sdb1
Device names depend on the order disks are detected. They can change between boots.
A mount command in ~/.bashrc
That runs only when that user opens a shell, not at boot, and needs root anyway.
An entry in /etc/mtab
/etc/mtab shows what's mounted right now. It isn't read at boot.

quiz.q: A script must stop with an error if the cp command just before this line failed. Which test belongs right after cp?
o: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then exit 1; fi
Right. $? holds the exit status of the last command; anything other than 0 means it failed.
if [ $# -ne 0 ]; then exit 1; fi
$# is how many arguments the script got, not whether cp worked.
if [ $0 -ne 0 ]; then exit 1; fi
$0 is the script's own name.
if [ $! -ne 0 ]; then exit 1; fi
$! is the PID of the last background job.

quiz.q: A contractor's account must stop working automatically at the end of Dec 31, 2026, but stay usable until then. Which command?
o: chage -E 2026-12-31 contractor
Right. -E sets the account expiration date. usermod -e does the same.
passwd -l contractor
That locks the password right now.
chage -M 90 contractor
-M sets the maximum password age, forcing a password change, not an account end date.
userdel contractor
That deletes the account immediately.

quiz.q: Which crontab line runs /opt/backup.sh at 2:30 a.m. every weekday, Monday through Friday?
o: 30 2 * * 1-5 /opt/backup.sh
Right. Minute 30, hour 2, any day of the month, any month, weekdays 1 to 5.
2 30 * * 1-5 /opt/backup.sh
Minute comes first. This tries hour 30, which doesn't exist.
30 2 1-5 * * /opt/backup.sh
1-5 in the third field means days 1 to 5 of each month, not weekdays.
30 14 * * 1-5 /opt/backup.sh
Hour 14 is 2:30 p.m.

quiz.q: You want only error-level (and worse) messages from the SSH service since yesterday. Which command?
o: journalctl -u sshd -p err --since yesterday
Right. -u picks the unit, -p err keeps priority err and higher, --since sets the start time.
journalctl -k -p err
-k shows kernel messages only.
tail -f /var/log/messages | grep sshd
It follows new lines only and can't filter by priority.
dmesg | grep sshd
dmesg is the kernel ring buffer. sshd's messages aren't there.

quiz.q: A host is 172.16.5.130/25. What is its network address, and how many usable host addresses does that subnet have?
o: 172.16.5.128, with 126 usable hosts
Right. A /25 splits the last octet into blocks of 128 (.0 and .128). 128 addresses minus network and broadcast leaves 126.
172.16.5.0, with 254 usable hosts
That's a /24. With /25, .130 falls in the upper half.
172.16.5.128, with 128 usable hosts
128 is the block size. Two addresses go to the network and broadcast.
172.16.5.130, with 126 usable hosts
The network address is where the block starts, .128, not the host's own address.

quiz.q: App servers on the network can't connect to the database. ss -tlnp on the database server shows this. What's the MOST likely cause?
o: PostgreSQL is listening only on localhost, so remote connections are refused
Right. 127.0.0.1 means only programs on the same machine can reach it. It needs to listen on the server's network address.
The firewall blocks port 5432
Possible on some servers, but this output already shows a cause: it isn't listening on the network at all.
The database service isn't running
It's running and listening, just not on a network address.
DNS can't resolve the database server's name
Nothing here points to DNS. The listener itself is local only.

quiz.q: As part of a hardening review, you need every SUID-root regular file on the system. Which command?
o: find / -perm -4000 -user root -type f 2>/dev/null
Right. -perm -4000 matches files with the SUID bit set (along with any other bits), owned by root.
find / -perm -2000 -user root -type f 2>/dev/null
2000 is SGID, not SUID.
find / -perm -1000 -type f 2>/dev/null
1000 is the sticky bit.
chmod -R u-s /
That REMOVES the SUID bit from everything and would break programs like passwd and sudo.

quiz.q: A vendor sent report.pdf and report.pdf.sig, and you've imported their public key. Which command checks that the file wasn't changed AND came from them?
o: gpg --verify report.pdf.sig report.pdf
Right. It checks the detached signature against the file using the vendor's public key.
gpg --decrypt report.pdf
The file isn't encrypted, and decrypting doesn't prove who sent it.
sha256sum report.pdf
A hash shows whether the file changed only if you have a trusted hash to compare. It says nothing about who sent it.
gpg --sign report.pdf
That signs the file with YOUR key. It doesn't check theirs.

pbqs.title: Same task, two package families
pbqs.scenario: Your shop runs Ubuntu and Rocky Linux servers. For each task, pick the command for each family.

rows.req: Install nmap from the configured repositories.
rows.why: apt-get install nmap on Debian; dnf install nmap on Rocky (yum on older releases).
dpkg -S /usr/bin/curl and rpm -qf /usr/bin/curl both map a file to its package.

rows.req: List every file the openssh-server package installed.
rows.why: dpkg -L openssh-server and rpm -ql openssh-server list a package's files.

rows.req: Install a vendor's agent from a downloaded package file.
rows.why: dpkg -i agent.deb and rpm -i agent.rpm install a local file. (dnf install ./agent.rpm also works and pulls dependencies.)

rows.req: Refresh the list of available packages before patching.
rows.why: apt-get update downloads fresh package lists; dnf check-update refreshes metadata and shows pending updates.

pbqs.title: Triage six server problems
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a different server ticket. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two are distractors.

items.log:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda3        20G   20G     0 100% /var
items.why: /var is at 100%. Logs and databases there will start failing. Find the space with du and clean or grow it.

items.log: kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4812 (java) total-vm:8123456kB, anon-rss:6020112kB
items.why: The kernel's OOM killer ended the biggest process to free memory. Check free -m and the app's memory settings.
MySQL accepts connections only from the same host. Remote app servers will be refused until it listens on a network address.
A SUID-root copy of bash hidden in /tmp gives anyone a root shell. Classic attacker persistence: escalate it as an incident.

items.log: 10.20.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.0.15
items.why: Only the local subnet route exists. With no default route, the host can't reach anything off 10.20.0.0/24.

items.log: EXT4-fs error (device sdb1): ext4_lookup:1601: inode #131074: comm ls: deleted inode referenced: 131590
items.why: The kernel found file system corruption. Unmount the file system and run fsck (e2fsck) on it.

keep.text: LPIC-1 stays active for 5 years. Renew it by passing the current 101 and 102 again, by earning LPIC-2 (which renews LPIC-1 to the same date), or with an LPI membership plus 20 professional development units (PDUs) a year.
keep.after: Your LPIC-1 must still be active when you earn LPIC-2.

keep.text: LPIC-1 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix, so on its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: Pair it with a cert that is on the matrix, such as Security+. Some positions also want proof you can run the operating system you'll manage, and LPIC-1 shows that for Linux.

keep.text: Most cloud servers run Linux. LPIC-1 plus an AWS or Azure cert is a strong pair for cloud admin and cloud security jobs.
keep.after: Use CG COOL for both vouchers.
